title: What should you ask first in a revenue drop case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a revenue drop case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first which revenue stream, customer segment or region is falling, because a total revenue figure hides where the drop really comes from. The trap is explaining revenue as one number, and jumping to fixes before you know which piece moved.
body:
The first question to ask

Which stream, segment or region is falling, and since when?

Revenue is almost never down evenly. One product, one customer group or one region usually accounts for most of the drop, and the others may even be growing. Find that piece first and the rest of the case gets much smaller. Also ask whether competitors are seeing the same thing: a market-wide fall points to demand, a client-only fall points to the client's offer or execution.

How to build your structure

  1. Split revenue into its streams (products, segments, regions) and find which one fell.
  2. Break that stream into number of customers × spend per customer.
  3. Look for the cause in four places: the market, customers, competitors and the company itself.

For a cinema chain with revenue down 12%, that means tickets, food and drink, and advertising first. Then tickets become visits × average price. Flat visits with lower food spend per visit is a very different problem from fewer people coming at all.

"Revenue is made of a few streams, so I'd first find which one fell, then split it into number of customers and spend per customer."

Go beyond the average

A software company's annual revenue fell from $20M to $18M, down 10%. Split by segment:

SegmentLast yearThis yearChange
Enterprise$12M$13M+$1M
Small business$8M$5M−$3M
Total$20M$18M−$2M

Enterprise is growing. Small business has lost more than the whole net decline. A company-wide price rise or a broad marketing push would treat both the same and miss the point.

Now split small business into customers × spend. Average spend held at about $2,000 a year, so customers fell from 4,000 to 2,500. That fall has two possible sources: fewer new customers, or more leaving. Ask for the flows. If 700 joined and 2,200 left (4,000 + 700 − 2,200 = 2,500), the story is churn, not acquisition, and the next question is why small customers are leaving.

The trap most people fall into

Treating revenue as one number. It leads to generic fixes, such as "run promotions" or "hire more sales staff", that may target the part of the business that is fine.

Weak: "Revenue is down 10%, so the client should invest in marketing to win back customers."
Strong: "Enterprise is up $1M and small business is down $3M, so the problem sits entirely in small business. Do we know whether that's fewer sign-ups or more customers leaving?"

The fix is a habit: before saying why, say where, and attach a dollar figure to it.

Two prompts to try

A pharma company's new drug is selling 40% below forecast.

Show the answer
  • Doctors: awareness and trust in the trial data; who prescribes, specialists or family doctors.
  • Patients: how many are diagnosed and eligible, and whether the forecast was realistic; price, side effects, stopping early.
  • Payers: approval for reimbursement; restrictions such as "only after other drugs fail".
  • Competition: rival drugs and generics; their pricing and contracts.

Where to start: payers. If insurers or health systems restrict the drug, doctors and patients can do little about it.

The trap: assuming it is a marketing problem before checking access and reimbursement.

A software company's monthly customer churn has doubled from 1% to 2%.

Show the answer
  • Who is leaving: by size, plan and account age; new customers versus long-standing ones.
  • Why they leave: product gaps, bugs, a price rise; moved to a competitor or stopped needing it.
  • When: after onboarding, at renewal, after a recent release or price change.
  • What we do about it: onboarding and support; contracts, pricing, customer success.

Size it first: 2% a month compounds to about 22% of customers lost a year, against about 11% before.

Where to start: who is leaving. Churn is rarely spread evenly, so find the segment.

The trap: jumping to retention discounts before knowing who leaves and why.
